 Merck Manuals Helps Patients Navigate the Different Types of Sunscreens
 News provided by
 The Merck Manuals
 Oct 29, 2026, 08:00 ET
 Share this article
 Share this article
 RAHWAY, N.J. , Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- When it comes to safeguarding your skin from the sun, sunscreen is an important part of year-round protection. Yet not all sunscreens are created equal. Getting the necessary protection depends on choosing the right kind of sunscreen.
 In a new editorial from MerckManuals.com , Jonette E. Keri, MD, PhD, University of Miami, Miller School of Medicine, shares key information about different types of sunscreens, including chemical and mineral varieties. She also shares sunscreen usage tips.
 Chemical versus mineral sunscreens 
 Sunburn results from a brief overexposure to ultraviolet (UV) light. Most sunscreens are designed to protect against UVA and UVB light, says Keri. Chemical sunscreens work by absorbing UV rays and converting that energy into heat. Mineral or barrier sunscreens, which contain zinc oxide or titanium dioxide, work by reflecting both UVB and UVA rays.
 Some people have concerns about the safety and absorption of sunscreen ingredients, says Keri. Studies have shown some systemic absorption of certain chemical sunscreen ingredients, but there is no current evidence  that this is harmful to humans. Others may have similar concerns about systemic absorption of nanoparticle mineral-based sunscreens. People concerned about the effects of absorbed nanoparticles may prefer to use so-called "non-nano" mineral sunscreens, says Keri.
 More details on bemotrizinol 
 One sunscreen ingredient in particular has been the subject of headlines in the United States recently. Bemotrizinol is a chemical blocker that has been used as a sunscreen ingredient in Europe and other parts of the world for years, says Keri. In June 2026, the FDA approved  bemotrizinol for use as an over-the-counter sunscreen active ingredient.
 This single ingredient provides both UVA and UVB coverage. Bemotrizinol is also more stable when exposed to sunlight than currently available UVA sunscreen ingredients in the United States. And because it is a larger molecule, there is very little absorption through the skin, says Keri.
 Sunscreen usage tips 
 Ultimately, the best sunscreen is the one you're going to use, says Keri. But for best protection, use a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with an SPF rating of 30 or higher.
 Here are a few additional sunscreen tips:
 Reapply sunscreen every two hours and immediately after swimming, sweating, or drying off.
 If using a spray-on product, apply outdoors to avoid inhaling the product.
 Use enough sunscreen for adequate protection – roughly the amount of a shot glass full for the body and a quarter-sized amount for the face and neck.
 Make sure to apply sunscreen to often-forgotten areas, such as the scalp and hairline, ears, backs of the hands and tops of the feet.
 To read more of Keri's insights on sunscreen and sun protection, visit the editorial at MerckManuals.com .
 About The Merck Manuals and MSD Manuals 
 First published in 1899 as a pocket-sized reference for physicians and pharmacists, The Merck Manual has evolved into one of the world's most trusted and widely-used medical resources. Available in 16 languages and reaching nearly 250 countries, The Manuals offer far more than text.
